text: Today's talk is going to start off with just a brief look at GTM engineering and what it is, and then I'm gonna get into kind of the areas that I consider to be the most technically interesting and challenging within this space.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So GTME is pretty new.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's arosen out of a couple factors, but one of the main motivating ones is that GTM teams have kind of realized that it is now possible to ship as fast as a product and engineering team.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so the best GTM teams that I work with are generally pushing changes to their GTM structure almost at the same cadence that an engineering team might be doing releases.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so at Clay, what that looks like is something like this, where every two weeks we are pushing new data to our teams, we are pushing new automations, we're, of course, running new campaigns, and we're constantly iterating on the things that we're shipping and trying to keep pace with the speed that our engineering team is working at.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So to do this, you need a couple fundamentals in place.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And in my view, GTM engineering at its heart is really about removing the constraints that have historically stopped GTM teams from shipping at speed using technology.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the role itself has exploded.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I would venture to say that most advanced GTM teams are now hiring GTM engineers or looking for this role.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And in my opinion, it's one of the first roles that actually is an index on the advances that we're making in AI.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so as models have become more powerful, GTM engineers have gained more leverage within their organization and become more valuable.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we've seen tremendous growth in this role.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I kind of break it down into four areas.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what I hope to do with this talk is kind of lightning round, go through some of the technical problems and solutions that I see for this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you're not familiar with Clay, we are obviously building infrastructure that kind of attacks these areas.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But this is not meant to be a sales pitch.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's more meant to be, if you're an engineer or a GTM engineer that's working on these things, some ways to think about how to structure it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then if you're a founder in the space, some of the interesting problems that I think are worth tackling.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the first is data.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And more than most teams within a company, data is the lifeblood of GTM.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the core goal that I think we're trying to accomplish with our data is to create a perfect virtual copy of the market, the ideal customers, the accounts, the context that you're going after.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So most teams start out with something that looks like this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You have accounts, which are the companies that you're targeting, and contacts, which are the people that you're going after.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The problem, though, that makes this challenging is that accounts at least exist in a state of constant change.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As an organization, a company might be getting acquired.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It might be spinning up new offices.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It might be launching new products.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the company itself is always changing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In addition, you as the GTM team are doing things to the company that it's making it change as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you're marketing at them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You're selling towards them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You're trying to book meetings.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's changing the state of the account.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then also the company itself is hiring people and firing people and doing things that provide signals for you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So as GTM engineers, we need to manage all of this state within our accounts, and we don't have all the data that we need to do this kind of right off the bat.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is what an example from Clay's CRM looks like.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can see I have a ton of fields that are simply telling me what state this account is in, whether they're a customer or not, whether they're expanding or churning, how big they are, how well they're scoring.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so one of the fundamental things that we need to do is make sure that our records are updated so that we can accurately action on what's happening here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so in a brand new CRM or a CRM that I'm going into, the first thing that I am doing is actually filling up the account with relevant contacts, and then I'm layering in third-party information that is gonna help me figure out which accounts to target and which ones are in market.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Primarily I'm looking at the account hierarchy, the firmographics that describe how big the company is and so forth, the technographics that describe what technology they're using, and then I'm trying to create signals on top of those accounts that are going to allow me to go after that company.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so because there's a lot of third-party data involved here, we need to actually go out and source and procure that data.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And within GTM, there is literally hundreds of vendors that you can turn to to get the data that you need, but none of those vendors is gonna have a complete picture of all the information you desire.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so the key technique here is called waterfalling.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is where I'm going to actually go and look into multiple providers to try to fill in all the information that I need.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you see here, if I was just using Forager to get phone numbers for this set of countries, I'd only get halfway there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So instead what I need to do is layer on all of these other providers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's not only true for phone numbers, but for most of the other data points that we care about within GTM.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so either you or the vendor that you're using needs to run evals against these data providers in order to obtain the most accurate information.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so not only do I need to sync in third-party information to my data layer, I also need to incorporate first-party information, and I need to keep that constantly up to date.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's also incredibly expensive to update data all the time, especially if you're purchasing it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I can't just update all the fields, I need to kind of selectively choose which fields to update.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And not only am I pulling information from various sources, but if I'm running a signals program, information that I need is getting pushed to me all the time as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And because I'm using multiple third-party sources, the actual representation of a single account in those different sources is gonna be different.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I need to resolve the entities in between them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so a great data layer will tackle all of these things and allow me to kind of move on to the more interesting work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But without this, it's really, really hard to execute automated GTM plays.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the next piece that I need to get right is orchestration.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this occurs because within GoToMarket there are literally dozens of tools that most teams are using.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I might have a sequencer or a dialer or a bunch of places where my reps are living or my field marketing is living.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And in most cases, the view of the world that those tools have is different depending on where you look.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so orchestration, in my view, is really the act of keeping all that up to date.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so what happens to our data model then is I'm, on top of my enriched information, I'm sending emails and calling into my contacts, the account is generating events that I need to keep track of, and I now need a system to actually plug all this into my data layer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so most teams are going to have something that looks like this as their basic stack, CRM, data warehouse, sequencer, a dialer, a note taker for call recording, and some chat interface like Slack.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: However, I usually see like 10 or 20 or 30 tools that actually these teams are interfacing with, and orchestration needs to kind of keep that information up to date.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The problem with orchestration is all of these different systems have different data needs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So some systems need kind of like real-time updates, one record at a time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Other systems are gonna need hundreds of thousands of records, maybe updated once a day.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I might need to schedule updates on a monthly or weekly basis depending on the data I'm using.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Some data points like employee count change all the time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Other data points like headquarters location change very rarely.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I'm not going to be making updates to all the fields at the same time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I need logic within these systems that helps with that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I also need to be able to take a single system that I'm working with and actually fan its information out to multiple different systems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And because I end up with this kind of distributed setup, I also have failures that are happening all the time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this turns into a fairly complex data engineering problem that we need to resolve.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A classic example of this is when I'm working with these different systems, usually they are not fully orchestrated, which means that one system is talking to each other while I'm trying to talk to both of those systems at the same time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So for example, if you have a Salesforce connected to outreach or a sequencer, usually that CRM and that sequencer are syncing independently of your orchestration system.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so if you create contacts in your CRM, you actually need to wait for that contact to sync
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: to the sequencer before you can then take action on it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This creates some difficult problems where you actually need to introduce things like waits and loops to check if information is ready.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So Clay, we've iterated on this problem quite a bit, and we've ended up in a place where we are basically taking a graph-based view of the orchestration problem with a series of general-purpose nodes that are executing various things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we have nodes that run agents, nodes that make tool calls, nodes that handle our conditional logic, nodes that run code, and the nodes that run effectively this MapReduce system to fan out the information and bring it back.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so a great orchestration layer will handle all of these, and whether you buy it or build it, I think this is fundamentally the kind of modern way to set this up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here's an example of this in Clay, and again, you can use other tools for this, but basically I'm going to have some sort of event that kicks off my orchestration, some trigger or some schedule.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm going to then talk to a couple different systems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm gonna combine that information back together, and then I'm gonna push it out to different interfaces that my reps are using.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Okay, so now that I have a data layer set up and I have my everything orchestrated, I now have this system which is starting to look a lot more complex.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And if you spend a lot of time in GoToMarket, I think this is actually like one of the simplest views of what is happening with an account.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Where I have multiple signals that are occurring.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I have data that needs to be updated.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I have actions that my agents or reps are taking.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then I have meetings that are happening and feedback that's occurring.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so the state of the world today is that we are relying on sales reps in a lot of cases to manually sort through this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But one of the great advances in the last year or so is that we can now use agents to take care of all this context.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: However, if you use agents, you actually run into some of the same problems that you are dealing with if you just use LLMs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So in GTM in particular, we are trying to build very long-running agents, agents that run over a course of weeks or months that keep track of the state of an account throughout a deal cycle.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We also have a high bar for error because a lot of the results of our GTM work is customer communication, and getting that wrong can have disastrous consequences.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then finally, the agents are often doing unstructured work and pushing that into systems that are highly structured like a CRM.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so the mapping of what the agent is producing is super important.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the architecture that we've landed on for this that I think is most powerful is an agent that exists for each account and maintains a persistent state of that account.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's always going to execute, and because it's executing over a course of weeks or months, it's often gonna be dormant for most of the time that it's available.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we need to use smart triggers or a heartbeat or something to wake it up, and then when it wakes up, it needs to kind of ingest the current context of the account from our data layer and our orchestration layer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And because the agent is making decisions for us in many cases automatically we need to allow for feedback on the agent as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The cutting edge of doing this is the learning phase where as the agent works on an account or a series of accounts it updates its own view of what's working.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Today in GTM this is not fully solved yet and in fact the continual learning effort and the next best action suggestions are kind of one of the cutting edge problems that we're working on.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00
